title: Computer Hardware – Peripherals and Components
content:
Computer Hardware – Peripherals and Components

Input Peripherals

DeviceDescription
KeyboardMost common input device; enters text and commands.
MousePoints and clicks on-screen objects (GUI).
ScannerCaptures hardcopy (paper) and converts to digital.
MicrophoneCaptures audio input.
WebcamCaptures video images.
TouchscreenActs as both input AND output device.
OMR ReaderReads marks on specially designed forms (e.g., exam sheets).
OCR ReaderReads printed/handwritten characters.
RFID ReaderReads radio tags (e.g., library books, access cards).
QR Code ReaderReads 2D barcodes containing encoded information.
Biometric sensorFingerprint, iris, face recognition.

Output Peripherals

DeviceDescription
Monitor/VDUDisplays visual output. LED, LCD, OLED types.
PrinterProduces hardcopy output (paper). Inkjet, laser, 3D.
SpeakersOutput audio.
PlotterDraws precise line drawings; used in CAD/engineering.
3D PrinterCreates 3D physical objects from digital designs.
ActuatorConverts electrical signals into physical movement (used in control systems).

Internal CPU Components

  • ALU (Arithmetic Logic Unit): Performs arithmetic (+, -, ×, ÷) and logic (comparisons) operations.
  • Control Unit (CU): Fetches, decodes, and executes instructions; coordinates all CPU activities.
  • Registers: Small, fast storage locations inside the CPU. Examples: Program Counter (PC), Accumulator (ACC), Instruction Register (IR), MAR, MDR.
  • Cache Memory: Very fast memory between CPU and RAM. Stores frequently used data.

Machine Instruction Cycle (Fetch-Decode-Execute)

  1. Fetch: Control unit fetches next instruction from RAM into the CPU.
  2. Decode: Control unit decodes the instruction to understand what it means.
  3. Execute: ALU or appropriate unit executes the instruction.

Storage Devices

DeviceTypeNotes
RAMPrimary, VolatileStores currently running programs; lost on power off.
ROMPrimary, Non-volatileStores BIOS; cannot be changed by user.
Hard Disk Drive (HDD)SecondaryMagnetic storage; large capacity, slower.
Solid State Drive (SSD)Secondary, Solid-stateFast, no moving parts; expensive per GB.
USB Flash DriveSecondary, Solid-statePortable; plug and play.
Optical Disc (CD/DVD)SecondaryReads/writes using laser.

title: Data Communication and Computer Networks
content:
Data Communication and Computer Networks

1. Communication Modes

ModeDirectionExample
SimplexOne direction onlyTV broadcast, keyboard to computer
Half DuplexBoth directions, but not simultaneouslyWalkie-talkie
Full DuplexBoth directions simultaneouslyTelephone call, video call

2. Network Types

TypeFull NameCoverageExample
PANPersonal Area Network~10 metresBluetooth devices
LANLocal Area NetworkBuilding/campusSchool network
MANMetropolitan Area NetworkCityCity cable network
WANWide Area NetworkCountry/worldInternet

3. Network Topologies

  • Bus: All devices connected to a single cable. Simple but single point of failure.
  • Star: All devices connect to a central hub/switch. Most common; easy to manage.
  • Ring: Each device connected to two others in a circle. Data travels in one direction.
  • Mesh: Every device connected to every other. Highly fault-tolerant but expensive.

4. Network Devices

DeviceFunction
HubSends data to all connected devices (no intelligence).
SwitchSends data only to the target device (intelligent hub).
RouterConnects different networks; directs data packets between them.
ModemModulates/demodulates signals for internet connection.
RepeaterBoosts signal strength over long distances.
BridgeConnects two similar networks together.

5. Network Protocols

ProtocolPurpose
TCP/IPMain internet protocol; handles addressing and data transmission
HTTP/HTTPSWeb browsing (HTTPS is secure)
FTPFile transfer
SMTPSending emails
POP3/IMAPReceiving emails
DNSTranslates domain names to IP addresses

title: Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra
content:
Logic Gates and Boolean Algebra

1. Logic Gates

A logic gate is an electronic circuit with one or more inputs and one output, performing a basic logic operation. Logic 1 = HIGH = True; Logic 0 = LOW = False.
GateSymbolOperationOutput Rule
ANDD-shape with flat backA AND BOutput is 1 ONLY if ALL inputs are 1
ORCurved shield shapeA OR BOutput is 1 if ANY input is 1
NOTTriangle with circleNOT AOutput is opposite of input
NANDAND + circle at outputNOT(A AND B)Output is 0 ONLY if ALL inputs are 1
NOROR + circle at outputNOT(A OR B)Output is 1 ONLY if ALL inputs are 0
XOROR with extra curveA XOR BOutput is 1 if inputs are DIFFERENT
XNORXOR + circleNOT(A XOR B)Output is 1 if inputs are the SAME

2. Truth Tables

ABANDORNANDNORXORXNOR
00001101
01011010
10011010
11110001

3. De Morgan's Laws

First Law: NOT(A AND B) = (NOT A) OR (NOT B)
Second Law: NOT(A OR B) = (NOT A) AND (NOT B)
These laws allow you to simplify logic expressions and substitute gates.

4. Boolean Algebra Laws

  • Identity: A AND 1 = A; A OR 0 = A
  • Null: A AND 0 = 0; A OR 1 = 1
  • Idempotent: A AND A = A; A OR A = A
  • Complement: A AND NOT A = 0; A OR NOT A = 1
  • Double Negation: NOT(NOT A) = A

title: Number Systems
content:
Number Systems

Common Number Systems

SystemBaseDigits UsedUse
Binary20, 1Computer's native language
Octal80–7Compact representation
Decimal100–9Everyday use
Hexadecimal160–9, A–FMemory addresses, colour codes

Converting Between Number Systems

Decimal to Binary

Repeatedly divide by 2 and read remainders from bottom to top.
Example: 25 ÷ 2 = 12 r1 → 12 ÷ 2 = 6 r0 → 6 ÷ 2 = 3 r0 → 3 ÷ 2 = 1 r1 → 1 ÷ 2 = 0 r1
25₁₀ = 11001₂

Binary to Decimal

Multiply each bit by its place value (powers of 2) and add.
Example: 1011₂ = (1×8) + (0×4) + (1×2) + (1×1) = 8+0+2+1 = 11₁₀

Hexadecimal Digits

HexDecimalBinary
0–90–90000–1001
A101010
B111011
C121100
D131101
E141110
F151111

Hex to Binary

Replace each hex digit with its 4-bit binary equivalent.
Example: 2E₁₆ → 2=0010, E=1110 → 00101110₂

Octal to Binary

Replace each octal digit with its 3-bit binary equivalent.
Example: 7₈ = 111₂; 326₈ = 011 010 110₂

ASCII Code

ASCII (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) assigns a unique 7-bit binary code to each character (letters, digits, symbols).

Example: 'A' = 65₁₀ = 01000001₂; 'a' = 97₁₀

title: Web Authoring – HTML
content:
Web Authoring – HTML (HyperText Markup Language)

HTML is the standard language used to create web pages. It uses tags (enclosed in angle brackets) to structure content.

Basic HTML Structure

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
  <head>
    <title>My Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello World</h1>
  </body>
</html>

Common HTML Tags

TagPurpose
<h1>–<h6>Headings (h1 = largest)
<p>Paragraph
<a href="">Hyperlink
<img src="">Image
<ul> / <ol>Unordered / Ordered list
<li>List item
<table>Table
<tr>Table row
<td>Table data cell
<th>Table header cell
<br>Line break
<hr>Horizontal rule (dividing line)
<b> / <strong>Bold text
<i> / <em>Italic text
<!-- -->Comment

HTML Attributes

Attributes provide additional information about elements. They appear inside the opening tag.

Examples:
<a href="https://example.com" target="_blank">Click here</a>
<img src="photo.jpg" alt="Description" width="200">
<p style="color:red;">Red text</p>

HTML Lists

Unordered list (<ul>): Bullet points
Ordered list (<ol>): Numbered list
Each item uses <li> tag.
